BOOK THREE The Delphic Apollo, through the responses of the Pythia, declared Socrates the wisest of all men. He, moreover, is recorded to have said, prudently and most learnedly, that the breasts of men ought to have been windowed and open, so that they might hold their thoughts not hidden but laid open for examination. Would indeed that the nature of things, following his opinion, had made them unfolded and plainly visible! For had it been so, not only would the merits or vices of minds be seen ready to hand, but also the knowledge of the disciplines, placed under the scrutiny of the eyes, would be approved by no uncertain judgements. And to the learned and the knowledgeable an eminent and lasting authority would be added, and the artificers themselves would draw clients by their own expertise. Even if they were not abundant in money, nor had gained renown from the long standing of their workshops, nor even through favour in the forum and eloquence, they could, once they were prepared, hold authority in proportion to the diligence of their studies, so that what they profess to know would be believed of them. Therefore, since these things have been established not thus, but as the nature of things willed, it does not come about that men, the talents being obscured beneath the breasts, can judge the sciences of the crafts, lying deeply hidden as they are, as they truly are.

We can observe this most of all in the case of the ancient sculptors and painters. Of these, those who held the marks of distinction and the favour of recommendation remain in everlasting memory for posterity: Myron, Polycletus, Phidias, Lysippus and the others who attained renown from their art. For they obtained this according as they made works for great cities, or for kings, or for noble citizens. But those who were of no less zeal, talent and skill, and who made works no less excellently finished for citizens noble but of humble fortune, attained no memory. This was because they were abandoned not by industry nor by skill in their art but by good fortune: such were Hegias of Athens, Chion of Corinth, Myagrus of Phocaea, Pharax of Ephesus, Boedas of Byzantium, and many others besides. Next, as was first and necessary, I explained by reasoned arguments, concerning city walls, how healthy sites are to be chosen; and I showed by linear diagrams what the winds are and from which quarters each of them blows; and I taught how the layouts of the avenues and streets within the walls are to be correctly made; and thus I set the limit of the first book. Likewise in the second I treated of building material: what advantages it has in works, and with what properties it has been furnished by the nature of things. Now in the third I shall speak of the sacred temples of the immortal gods and set them out, fully described, as is proper.

Unit Vitr.3.1.1-3.1.2 (Vitr. 3.1.1–3.1.2). ENGLISH:
The composition of temples consists in symmetry, the principle of which architects ought to hold to most diligently. This, moreover, is produced by proportion, which in Greek is called ἀναλογία. Proportion is the commodulation, by a fixed part, of the members in every work and of the whole, from which the principle of symmetries is brought about. For no temple can have a principle of composition without symmetry and proportion, unless it has an exact relation of its members like that of a well-shaped man. For nature has so composed the body of a man that the face, from the chin to the top of the forehead and the lowest roots of the hair, is a tenth part; likewise the open hand, from the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, just as much; the head, from the chin to the top of the crown, an eighth; from the top of the chest, together with the base of the neck, to the lowest roots of the hair, a sixth; from the middle of the chest to the top of the crown, a fourth. Of the height of the face itself, moreover, one third is from the bottom of the chin to the bottom of the nostrils; the nose, from the bottom of the nostrils to the boundary at the middle of the eyebrows, just as much; from that boundary to the lowest roots of the hair the forehead is formed, likewise of a third part. The foot, indeed, is a sixth of the height of the body, the cubit a fourth, the chest likewise a fourth. The remaining members also have their own proportions of commensuration, by making use of which the ancient painters and noble sculptors also attained great and boundless praise.

In the same way, the members of sacred temples ought to have, from their individual parts, a most fitting correspondence of commensuration to the general sum of the whole magnitude. Again, the central midpoint of the body is by nature the navel. For if a man is laid on his back with hands and feet spread out, and the centre of a pair of compasses is set on his navel, then in drawing the circle round, the fingers and toes of both hands and feet will be touched by the line. And no less than a circular figure is produced in the body, so also a square delineation will be found in it. For if one measures from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, and that measure is transferred to the outstretched hands, the breadth will be found to be the same as the height, as in areas that are squared by the set-square. Therefore, if nature has so composed the human body that its members correspond in their proportions to its entire configuration, the ancients appear to have laid it down with good reason that in the completion of works also there should be an exactness of commensuration of the individual members to the general appearance of the figure. Accordingly, while they handed down orderly arrangements for all works, they did so above all for the temples of the gods, because the praise and the blame for those works are wont to endure forever.

No less also, because a man's foot is the sixth part of his height (and so too, from the fact that the height of the body is completed by the number of feet, the base of the shaft in ancient columns, raised six times, determined their heights), they established that number as perfect, and they observed that the cubit consists of six palms and twenty-four digits. But later, when they observed that both numbers were perfect, both six and ten, they combined both into one and made the most perfect number, sixteen. Of this they found the foot to be the origin. Thus it comes about that the foot has sixteen digits, and the bronze denarius just as many asses.

The pseudodipteros is laid out so that there are eight columns each in the front and in the posticum, and fifteen each on the sides, counting the corner columns. The walls of the cella are to stand opposite the four middle columns in the front and in the posticum. Thus there will be a space of two intercolumniations plus the thickness of a column at its base, from the walls round to the outermost rows of columns. There is no example of this at Rome, but there is one at Magnesia, the temple of Diana by Hermogenes of Alabanda, and the temple of Apollo built by Menesthes. The dipteros is octastyle both in the pronaos and in the posticum, but around the temple it has double rows of columns, as is the Doric temple of Quirinus and the Ionic temple of Diana at Ephesus, set up by Chersiphron. The hypaethros is decastyle in the pronaos and in the posticum. In all other respects it has the same features as the dipteros, but in the interior it has columns doubled in height, that is in two tiers, set back from the walls so as to allow a passage round, like the porticoes of peristyles. The middle is open to the sky, without a roof. There are entrances with folding doors at either end, in the pronaos and in the posticum. Of this too there is no example at Rome, but at Athens there is the octastyle in the Olympian temple precinct.

There are, moreover, five species of temples, whose names are these: pycnostyle, that is, with close-set columns; systyle, with columns somewhat more widely spaced; diastyle, with columns set apart from one another more widely than is proper; araeostyle, with the spaces of the intercolumniations lying open sparsely; eustyle, with a correct distribution of the intervals. The pycnostyle, then, is the temple in whose intercolumniation the thickness of one and a half columns can be interposed, as is the temple of the Deified Julius, and that of Venus in the Forum of Caesar, and any others that are composed in this way. Likewise the systyle is the temple in which the thickness of two columns can be placed in the intercolumniation, and the plinths of the bases are equal in size to the space between two plinths, as is the temple of Fortuna Equestris by the stone theatre, and the others that are composed on the same principles.

Unit Vitr.3.3.6-3.3.7 (Vitr. 3.3.6–3.3.7). ENGLISH:
We must now give the principle of the eustyle, which is the most commendable and has its principles worked out with regard to use, to appearance and to strength. For the spaces in the intervals are to be made of two column-thicknesses and a quarter of a column's thickness, and the middle intercolumniation, one on the front and the other on the rear, of three column-thicknesses. In this way the building will have a graceful appearance in its design, the use of the entrance without obstructions, and dignity in the walk around the cella. The principle of this arrangement will be set out as follows. The front of the site established for the temple, if a tetrastyle is to be built, is to be divided into 11½ parts, excluding the crepidines and the projections of the bases; if it is to be of six columns, into 18 parts; if an octastyle is to be set up, it is to be divided into 24½. Likewise, of these parts, whether of the tetrastyle, the hexastyle or the octastyle, one part is to be taken, and this will be the module. One of these modules will be the thickness of the columns. Each of the intercolumniations, except the middle ones, is to be of two modules and a quarter of a module; the middle ones, on the front and the rear, one each, of three modules apiece. The height of the columns themselves is to be of 9½ modules. Thus, from this division, the intercolumniations and the heights of the columns will have a correct proportion.

Of this we have no example at Rome, but in Asia there is at Teos the hexastyle temple of Father Liber. These symmetries, moreover, were established by Hermogenes, who was also the first to devise the scheme of the octastyle, that is, of the pseudodipteral temple. For he removed from the symmetry of the dipteral temple the inner rows of columns, thirty-four in number, and by this method made a saving of expense and labour. In the middle he admirably created spaciousness for the walkway around the cella, and took nothing away from its appearance; rather, without any want of the superfluous elements being felt, he preserved the dignity of the whole work by its layout. For the scheme of the pteroma and the disposition of columns around a temple were devised so that the appearance might have dignity on account of the roughness (asperitatem) of the intercolumniations. Further, if a violent downpour of rain should unexpectedly overtake and shut in a crowd of people, they might have free room to wait, with spaciousness, within the temple and around the cella. How well these things are worked out in the pseudodipteral arrangements of temples! Hence Hermogenes seems to have achieved the effects of his works with acute and great ingenuity, and to have left behind sources from which posterity might draw the principles of the disciplines.

Unit Vitr.3.3.10-3.3.11 (Vitr. 3.3.10–3.3.11). ENGLISH:
In araeostyle temples the columns are to be made so that their thicknesses are one eighth part of their heights. Likewise in the diastyle the height of the column is to be measured off into eight and a half parts, and the thickness of the column is to be set at one part. In the systyle let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and of these let one be given to the thickness of the column. Likewise in the pycnostyle the height is to be divided into ten parts, and one part of it is to be made the thickness of the column. For the columns of a eustyle temple, as for those of the systyle, let the height be divided into nine and a half parts, and let one part of it be fixed as the thickness of the bottom of the shaft. In this way the system of the intercolumniations will be maintained in due proportion. For in the same measure as the spaces between the columns increase, the thicknesses of the shafts must be enlarged in proportion. If in the araeostyle the thickness were a ninth or a tenth part, the column will appear thin and meagre, because through the breadth of the intercolumniations the air consumes and diminishes the apparent thickness of the shafts. Conversely, in pycnostyles, if the thickness were an eighth part, the closeness and narrowness of the intercolumniations will produce a swollen and ungraceful appearance. Therefore one must follow the symmetries proper to the kind of work. Moreover, the corner columns are to be made thicker by a fiftieth part of their own diameter, because they are cut around by the air and appear more slender to those looking at them. Therefore where the eye deceives, the deficiency must be made good by calculation.

The contractions at the tops of the columns, at the hypotrachelia, seem to require the following rule. These tempering adjustments are added to the thicknesses on account of the interval of height over which the sight (species) of the climbing eye passes. Let the foundations of these works be dug down to the solid and into the solid, if it can be found, as far as shall seem proportionate to the size of the work, and let the whole site be built up with masonry as solid as possible. Above ground let walls be built under the columns, thicker by one half than the columns are to be, so that the lower parts may be firmer than the upper; these are called stereobates, for they receive the loads. The projections of the bases (spirae) should not extend beyond the solid; likewise above, the thickness of the wall is to be kept in the same manner. The intervals between, however, are to be vaulted over or made solid with rammed fill (festucationibus), so that they may be held apart.

For the higher the sight of the eye climbs, the less easily does it cut through the density of the air; and so, having dispersed over the extent of the height and been stripped of its strength, it reports to the senses an uncertain quantity of the modules. Therefore a supplement by calculation must always be added in the members of the symmetries, so that, when works are either in higher places or are themselves of more colossal size, they may keep a due proportion of magnitudes. The breadth of the architrave at the bottom, where it will lie above the capital, is to be made as great as the thickness of the top of the column beneath the capital will be; at the top, as great as the bottom of the shaft. The cymatium of the architrave is to be made a seventh part of its height, and the same amount in projection. The remaining part, apart from the cymatium, is to be divided into twelve parts, and the lowest fascia is to be made of three of these, the second of four, the topmost of five. Likewise the frieze (zophorus) above the architrave is to be a fourth part less high than the architrave; but if figures are to be represented on it, a fourth part higher than the architrave, so that the carvings may have impressiveness. Its cymatium is to be a seventh part of its height; the projection of the cymatia is to be as much as their thickness.

Above the frieze the dentil is to be made as high as the middle fascia of the architrave; its projection is to be as much as its height. The height of the tympanum, which is in the pediment, is to be made thus: the whole front of the cornice, from the outermost cymatia, is to be measured off into nine parts, and of these one part is to be set up in the middle as the apex of the tympanum, provided that it answers plumb to the architraves and the hypotrachelia of the columns below. And the upper cornices are to be set equal to the lower ones, apart from the simae. Above the cornices the simae, which the Greeks call ἐπαιετίδες, are to be made higher than the cornices by an eighth part of the cornices' height. All the members which are to be above the capitals of the columns, that is, architraves, friezes, cornices, tympana, pediments, acroteria, are to be inclined forward on the front by a twelfth part of their own respective height. The reason is that when we stand facing the fronts, if two lines are extended from the eye, and one touches the lowest part of the work and the other the highest, the one which touches the highest will be the longer. Thus, the longer the line of sight runs toward the upper part, the more it makes that part appear to lean backward. But when, as has been written above, they have been inclined forward on the front, then to the view they will appear to be true to the perpendicular and the set-square. The flutings of the columns are to be made twenty-four in number, hollowed out in such a way that when a set-square has been placed in the hollow of a fluting and turned about, it touches with its arms the edges of the flutings on the right and on the left, and the point of the set-square can travel round, touching the curvature throughout. The thicknesses of the flutings are to be made as great as the addition in the middle of the column will be found to be from the diagram.

On the simae, which are above the cornice on the sides of temples, lions' heads are to be carved, arranged in such a way that first they are marked out opposite the individual columns, and the rest are arranged at equal intervals, so that each corresponds to the middle of each tile.
